chunks.text: You're welcome. And can I just say thank you very much for bearing with us. I know that we've mulled you around repeatedly. It has not been within our power. It's been because the house has gone to extended hours, et cetera. So it's been frustrating for us, but I know it's been frustrating for you, so thank you. So we really appreciate it.

We are basically right up towards the end of our hearing part of it, part of the ports inquiry. But we really appreciate having you here because without that, there'll be a substantial gap in our knowledge. So what I thought I'd do is hand over to you for if you want to make some introductory remarks.

Yep. And then there will be plenty of questions. I know I've got a long line up. Simon knows that I ask lots of questions. Just given the questions on the RMA, so replacement, should I say? Yeah. Okay. But in your hands, Leon. Look, thank you very much. I don't know how much you know about MSC, but we're a- Tell us a bit anyway. Yeah Yeah, will do. We're a family-owned international shipping company, started in 1970 by Mr. Aponte with one ship, and grown since then to be the largest container carrier in the world.

Also the largest privately owned cruise operator in the world as well, as well as one of the largest port operators and one of the largest cargo operators in the world. So quite a success story from a global footprint perspective. Within New Zealand, we started off with one person working out of his laundry in Auckland in 1996. We celebrated 30 years in New Zealand last month- Nice... in June. So thank you very much.

All right. Good then. Really a great milestone achievement for us. Nice function that we had in Christchurch, where our head office is, with our team. We have 76 people in the country, so a fairly large local footprint. And then we have a number of people that support the business across in Fremantle, which is our head office for the region today.

So when we started off as MSC in New Zealand, we basically slot charted on board a vessel that was going across from here to Australia, and New Zealand was connected through Australia to the rest of the world. Today, we operate our own three dedicated services in New Zealand. Our flagship service being the Eagle, which we launched in February this year.

That's a direct link between New Zealand and the USA, and then connecting from Panama into the world as well. Mostly focused around Europe and Africa and the Med. Then we have the Southern Loop, which is a service that comes out of Melbourne and does the south up and connects into Wellington to feed into the Eagle, and also across into Australia, to connect to the world as well from there.

And then we have the Noumea Express, which it's all in the name, goes through Noumea and the islands, comes into Tauranga, and then goes back to Australia from there and does a loop. So that's essentially us in a nutshell in terms of where we've come from. We're very much interested in growing in New Zealand.

We have grown this year, with double-digit growth for us- Awesome... across the board. Particularly in Wellington, we've partnered very closely with Centreport this year, where we've actually seen a 350% increase in our throughput through Wellington, starting from February this year with the introduction of our Eagle service.

So Wellington is our hub that we operate with today, and our services connect from the rest of the country into Wellington and then load onto either the Southern Loop or the Eagle going deep sea from here. Cool. That's it. Thank you very much. That's good to get that.

And we will also get a Hansard, so we've got all those routes in particular because I'm not-- Let's kick ourselves off with questions. So Dan and then I'll take one. Thanks, Mr. Chair. Thanks, Leon. I appreciate you coming in again. Sorry for the delay in- No problem meeting with you. Just reading through your submission, you've got, I think, a pretty good articulation of some of the key issues in the sector.

Yep. How do we power up productivity? If we were to say to you, "What's the top three things that you want as a result of this inquiry for us to improve productivity of the sector?" And before I hand it over to you, just- Yeah... some of the previous submissions have talked about kind of encouraging more of a hub and spoke model- Mm-hmm... across the sector.

We've talked about getting more accurate data and measurement on productivity measures across port boards. There's been discussions about section, is it 98 of the- 198. 198. Yeah. So that has been an impediment to- That's all... productivity- Mm-hmm... from overseas operators.

Mm-hmm. That just gives you a flavor, but hand it over to you, what do you think we should be looking at from a government recommendations perspective on how they can improve productivity? Yeah. Okay. Thank you. And thanks for the background. I did watch some of the feeds before, so I've had a little bit of insight into the conversations.

Our belief is that there's not a one-size-fits-all solution to the challenge because actually, the dynamic footprint of New Zealand, the geographical footprint, and the challenges that come with that, represents particular challenges in each of the different ports. So I don't think there's a silver bullet that we can put out there and say, "If you do this one thing or these three things, that'll solve all of the challenges."

I think each port has its own constraints, and each port needs to grapple with that and figure out ways to be able to handle that challenge. We operate with both a hub and spoke and a direct mechanism today. So essentially, the evil is our hub and spoke, and we use Wellington as our hub for that service.

But then the Southern Group is also a direct option going from the likes of Bluff directly into Australia as well. So we have a bit of a hybrid policy. Globally, MSC is-- We focus very much on standalone services and creating direct optionality for our customers.

We have a little bit of a benefit in terms of we're over 1,000 container ships. So being 21, I think it's 21.5% of the global container market and having the world's largest fleet allows us to be a little bit more dynamic in that port-to-port pairing. What we find with the hub and spoke mechanism is that it's really good to connect the smaller ports into a larger system for the deep sea leg. It does add cost to the system, though, because it's extra handling that comes into it. And depending on where you are on that leg

of the pre-feeder service, it can add quite a lot of transit time onto your cargo. So it could be ten days around the New Zealand coast, plus potentially when that connecting vessel connects into the hub, another week as you wait for the weekly service to come through, depending on your connections hub. Now, part of the challenge as a carrier is when we look at these system designs that we've put in place, we try and limit those connection gaps as much as possible.

We need to give the port some time to be able to resource up and manage the flows of the cargo. But you don't want to try and have a vessel arriving on a Monday to connect on a vessel that departed on a Sunday. You want to try and have it arrive on a Sunday to connect to the vessel arrive on the Monday instead. The challenge that we have in New Zealand ports now is because of the challenges we've seen over the last sort of four to five years, there is no flexibility.

So all of the ports, or 90% of the ports are oversubscribed. There's not that ability as a carrier to sit there and go, "I'd like a Wednesday window in this port, followed by a Friday window in that port," because it connects in the most efficient manner possible. So what we end up seeing, and you can have a look at that on some of our routings, we actually have a bit of a higgledy-piggledy where we backtrack because we can't get a berth in that port. So we've got to go to the next port, come back to that port, load the cargo, and then go to the next port from there.

So creating a little bit of space in the terminals is paramount for us. It's a bit of a crude saying, but shipping happens. We have a lot of delays, especially around the New Zealand coast, especially this time of the year. And in order for us to recover, our optionality is very limited in New Zealand today.

We have the potential to be able to speed up the vessels, but we have to be conscious of emissions. So by significantly increasing that, you also increase emissions and you also increase cost that comes with that. So having that little bit of play within the ports to be able to say, "Well, yes, I'm late, but I'm only three hours late," as opposed to if you arrive late, you can't have a berth.

The next vessel's waiting for the berth, and you wait a week for that berth. So what you see happening today is carriers are doing a lot of omissions, ourselves included. Or we call it a COR, change of rotation, where instead of doing the most efficient route on a planned voyage, we change the route to be able to call the next port so we don't lose that berth as well because of the cascading impact.

So to me, it's about trying to find, for each one of those particular ports, what is the limiting factor around their productivity and how do we address that? How do we help them? Is it CapEx? Is it access to labor? Is it whatever might be the challenge that's creating that particular hub to or that particular port to have the constraints that it has.

And then also, there's a little bit of capacity around the coast that's not necessarily fully utilized today. And that's the reason why we partnered with Centreport, because they had quite a lot of capacity that was underutilized post the earthquake. And we've seen them gear up quite substantially. I mentioned it earlier on, from February to May this year versus February to May the year before, we've increased by 350% our volumes coming through here.

So from 8,000 containers to 38,000 containers hubbing through the port here, and that was capacity they had. They have invested. They put, I think, around about $15 million in, in terms of new reefer towers and employed 50 new staff to be able to manage the volume throughput. But they had the footprint, they had the capacity to be able to grow and the want and the commercial nous to be able to do that.

So that to me is an example of where we can do that in a safe environment, in a productive environment as well. Excellent. So just take from that answer, definitely optimizing and providing the flexibility within each port around docking and coming in and going. That's one.

Yep. The second thing I take from what you've just said is more of a port-by-port specific analysis on what's the limiting constraint. Yeah. So that's something that government can do is sort of port by port. Just rounding it off in terms of next cab off the rank or a third area that you think we need to be looking in?

It's something I've thought is missing for a while, and you can probably tell by my accent that I've got a bit of a different view on the outside world, if I can put it that way. Is that sort of that long-term thinking that centralized, disconnected from any political cycles, disconnected from any local drivers that might be the case that actually drive the infrastructure network for New Zealand that is thinking of NZ Inc and driving a uniformed approach where- We don't have unnecessary spend taking place in certain places, under-investment taking place in other

areas, and a sort of shared view so that we as industry can actually invest and know that's the 30-year plan because we're talking 30, 50-year investments that we need to make to be able to make it work. Right now, the way that we're doing is we're dealing with each port individually and we're trying to sort of make our own assumptions as to what that future- Yeah prospect looks like.

Good. Thank you. Mr. Chair. Thank you. Yeah, okay, Simon. We can begin. How much of that constraint around port efficiency or the flow of freight is down to connections to and from the ports, land connections to landside infrastructure and land ports and so on?

Because around New Zealand, we've got different rail and road configurations. When you look at Auckland, you come off the bottom of Stanley Street there, you drive a truck and trailer, and you end up in what appears to be a 19th century kind of bullet track, like winding your way around the waterfront. Then you've got to navigate cyclists who always have priority in New Zealand.

Yeah. Whereas I would've thought if we wanted a well-functioning link to the rest of the transport network, you might want a dedicated tunnel or something straight into the port for your heavies. So, how much of that is a constraint? Yeah, look, I think it's a very fair point. Scalability really comes off the back of rail, and being able to connect those nodes.

We can see the proof point in the Metroport and Tauranga development. That's really performed well. There's been a significant change there now, which is, in my opinion, performed better. So, that's a great example of how rail can enable those connections. There are some parts of the country where that doesn't make sense, and that's where having the blue corridor, the coastal connection, makes a lot of sense.

We've been serving Bluff pretty much from day one. We're the only container carrier that calls into Bluff, and that's a great example of very heavy cargo. You've got the Rio Tinto coming out of there and other produce from the area that it doesn't really make sense to try and haul that across anywhere. So, having a dedicated product that's there week in, week out enables that industry. So again, it's a little bit of a hybrid.

But 100% agree, there's a stranglehold going into and out of the various nodes that we have today, for sure. So the committee was going to take away something to feed back into the infrastructure system. It's making sure that the right investments are made in that connecting infrastructure, and sources for courses, but you're going to get the best bang for buck by building your rail capacity into ports- Completely agree... to move the most boxes in the shortest possible amount of time.

Completely agree, and I'd add it to that third point that I made in terms of having that centralized direction, centralized thought pattern because we see a number of ICDs today, inland container depots today, where you might have one port- Sorry, just tell us what's an ICD. Inland container depot. Right. So that's what you're talking about now, having that rail corridor.

Yeah. So having the container closer to the customer, they don't have a very long road leg. They can truck into the depot, get it empty, take it to their pack plant, pack it, put it back into the depot, and rail it into the port, or have a land bridge as well, like a truck leg. So what we see that has happened in the past is not happening necessarily too much today, but what has happened in the past is you've had different ports having similar ideas and building their own ICDs next door to each other.

There's only so much capital in New Zealand. Right. We need to think a little bit smarter and pool that resource. And how do we actually take that and go, "Well, actually, let's have it disconnected from the ports. Let's have a third party, whatever that might be, that operates that." It could be a port that operates it. It doesn't really make a difference. But instead of you investing $300 million and me investing $300 million, let's invest $450 million and save $150 million, and have a shared facility that serves everybody in that community, and

all the both importers and exporters that come through there. So, that's kind of where I say that that third point really stacks up in terms of being able to give us that 30-year, 50-year plan around how do we actually make the smart investments in the country? Oh, okay. So we could, let's say we go down that 30-year plan arrangement.

We manage to persuade the ports to be involved in that way or require the ports to be involved in that way. What is the certainty we've got that we know what you're doing and what the other shipping lines are doing which actually works in with that, as opposed to saying, "Well, we've just decided that you put all this infrastructure in," let's say out of Auckland, "We've decided we're going out of Tauranga instead because somehow we've got a better deal for it." What's to make sure that all the parts of the system are working together well?

Look, I can't talk for the other carriers. I can only talk for- No, let's just talk to your own arrangements... But, we will go where the cargo is. That's as simple as that. That's our business. That's what we focus on. We move international freight. So if the cargo is in a centralized hub, we'll go to a centralized hub. If the cargo is in a diversified hub, we'll go to a diversified hub.

So that's why I said earlier on today, we run a hybrid model where we have a hub and spoke, and we also have a direct port pay connect that we have in place because it's that diverse today within New Zealand. So, there's other ways of doing it as well. I mentioned earlier on that we have other parts of our business as well, and other carriers have other parts of their business as well.

I think we're top three or top five port operators in the world today as TIL, which is a part of our business. And so there's potential investment opportunities on that front as well. But to me, at the end of the day, it comes down to where the cargo is. If the cargo is moved into specifically an efficient hub that we can get a vessel in and get it out as quickly as possible, we'd go there.

So when we talk about hub and spoke- Mm-hmm... one of the interesting things is which ports you actually, as shipping lines, which ports you actually go to. One of the things we've had impressed on us is that the vessels are going to get larger. Some ports are not going to be able to cope with those, so that kind of cuts them out of being a place that those vessels can go to, because they simply physically can't accommodate them.

Hmm. But which ports do you end up-- You could make a decision. The one example we've had in particular is in the South Island, where Lyttelton appears to have aspirations to take the business out of Timaru and Port Otago. Mm-hmm. So who's getting to decide? Is it the freight provider, whether it's Fonterra or Kotahi? Are they going to decide which port it's going out of?

Are you going to decide? Are the ports going to compete amongst each other on price? How does that work? Because there are, as you indicated, some really significant investment proposals- Yes... which may be good investments or may be not very good investments. Yeah. I guess I'll answer that in a couple of phases.

To answer your core question in terms of who makes that decision, at the end of the day, it's the shipper and the importer. So if a large importer goes and builds a deconsolidation facility in Palmerston North, the cargo will move to Palmerston North, and they'll distribute from there. If they build a major hub in Lyttelton to support the plan that Lyttelton has, then the cargo will move there, and they'd be responsible for that.

So just to pick that one up. So if Lyttelton were to build, I'm using this as an example, if they were to build a hub, that's a port making an investment decision. Mm-hmm. Are you saying that that would necessarily derive a Kotahi, for example? So I'm going to take the produce out of Southland and send it through Lyttelton as opposed to- Mm-hmm... through South Port or- No, the shipper makes the decision at the end of it.

That's what I want to understand. Yeah The shipper makes the decision. So if the shipper is driving it, the shipper would have to be a part of that. So you say Kotahi, so Fonterra or Silver Fern Farms- Yeah... in conjunction with Kotahi and the other customers would then say, okay, as part of that project, I would imagine that those discussions would be made before putting a billion dollars in the ground.

And that's the point, yeah. Yes. Yeah, okay. But you have to have the cargo there because otherwise you're holding a white elephant. Yep. Indeed. In terms of the question around the vessels getting larger, I think we need to put that into context. Globally, vessels are definitely getting larger. 24,000, 25,000 TEU ships on the East-West trades are commonplace today.

And up until probably October last year, the new builds were 80%-plus weighted on 12,000 TEU and larger vessels. There's been a bit of a shift since then. So BIMCO released their latest report in February this year. They haven't updated it yet.

But they estimate that below 12,000 TEU ships have significantly ramped up in the new orders to the extent of about 33% of the new builds been in that 8,000 and below TEU capacity vessels. So there are new, smaller ships being built, and that's because not every port is ever going to-- Some ports have granite bottoms. They can't get down to 12, 14, and 16-meter drafts.

And those ports still have to be served. We still need to be able to connect into those hubs with the spokes. So there will still be vessels. There just won't be as many of them, and they won't be as efficient as a 24,000 TEU vessel once it's on the water. But when a 24,000 TEU vessel's alongside and you've got to load 10,000 TEU on board that vessel in two days, that takes up a lot of resource, and that takes up a lot of capital to be able to get to that stage.

So what you're saying is, is what you're saying that you will continue to service New Zealand with vessels which are appropriate size for the ports that you're going to? Correct. Yeah, okay. Right. Cool. Other questions before I go onto another area? Okay. Look, can I just ask you about the issue of windows? Yes.

And that is, we regularly get the-- I'd be interested in, first of all, in your observations about how on time your own vessels are. Mm-hmm. But also what happens when they get to New Zealand, what the flexibility is in the system. You mentioned the IMO and being able to speed up, et cetera. My understanding is that we have not yet, or our understanding is that we have not yet signed the IMO agreement.

Correct. Yes. And that looks parked because I don't think we're the only ones unhappy with it. But the ability to be able to get vessels on time in and out- Yeah... flexibility to be able to deal with those will be really helpful. And also how different ports deal with windows with vessels that arrive out of window, because I know Napier told me when I visited them, they said, "You got Wednesday.

You miss Wednesday this week, it's Wednesday next week." Yes. That's an interesting way of doing it, as opposed to, well, we'll take you when we can. So I'd be interested in your observations on that. Yeah, look, there's a lot to that question. So in terms of our schedule reliability, we actually recently made a change to our network because we weren't happy with the reliability on our previous service, the Wallaby- Mm-hmm... and moved to the Southern Loop.

And by doing that, we disconnected some of the more challenging areas. We found that the vessels were late coming out of China quite often. And then that's where the regulation kicks in, where we can't speed up deep sea. Within New Zealand, if we need to, we do. But that obviously comes at a significant cost and environmental impact that we bear in mind as well.

So there's definitely a challenge with vessels getting into the country on time. No country in the world today, I would hazard to guess, is 100% on time all the time. So it's 100%, yeah. I can't remember the exact number, but global schedule reliability is in the mid-60s, mid to high 60s.

That's global. That's global schedule reliability. Okay. It's not a- And specific to New Zealand, it's a global challenge that's ongoing with the geopolitical challenges that we see and having to navigate that, and also the volume growth that we've seen.

So there's definitely challenges getting into the country on time. That said, even when we do get in on time, we still leave late, and that's for a number of reasons. Worse than you. So is the reliability worse when you leave than it was when you got here? Yes. Yeah. So in our submission, we made the statement, and this is going back a number of years, but New Zealand used to be a country where we would be able to come in slightly delayed, not badly delayed, but recover that schedule around the coast because in 2015, we were a lot more productive

per crane and per vessel birth rate than what we are today. So you add to that the volume increase between 2015 and today, which is basis the FIG stats, which are only available up until March, so I only have quarter one data. But if you look at that versus 2015, same 12-month window, it's about 200,000 containers extra that we're doing at a lower productivity, which equates to 30% longer for ships being alongside in New Zealand. So that soaks up all of that flex that we had in the ports before, because no port would be efficient or would be

a healthy business if they had 30-plus percent unused capacity at any given time. Mm. 5%, 10% makes a lot of sense, and you can flex between them. You can actually use that capacity to recover delays and maybe you have additional project cargo or spot business or those kinds of things, then you can look at those opportunities, but that's just not there.

So what specifically has happened as far as you're aware that's reduced-- Because you're basically saying that we are less productive now- Yeah... per container move, crane hour, whatever, than we were a decade ago. Yeah. What's changed? Just the overall productivity in the ports has changed. Could you- And the volume has also lifted. Right, and the volume's- The volume's also lifted. So if we go 2015 to today, it's about 200,000 containers extra basis the FIG stats using the figs.

But are you saying that a crane today lifts less? Yes. Why? Do you know? Like I said earlier on, it's specific to each port that they have their constraints within it that drive the reasoning behind that. It might be that some-... ports have aging infrastructure, aging cranes that need a little bit more downtime, need a little bit of care.

It might be that some ports have struggled to resource the landside to feed the crane. Some might be a resourcing issue for the crane itself. There's multiple different reasons for each port, and I think if you speak to the ports, they would understand that for each of their ports specifically, or they should. The conversations we have with them, they definitely do.

Hmm. That's concerning to hear that particular... But anybody else got other questions for him? Or I carry on? Section 198- Yeah... you mentioned. Yep. Can you tell us about that? SWIs kind of made life a little bit easier in some ways, and since they decided they can't make it work at the moment.

But the optimal way in which you've already said you do some doubling back, but at the moment you're constrained in what you can do. What would the ideal arrangement be for you? In terms of Section 198, from a MSC perspective, we see our core task as international freight- Mm... not coastal freight.

Coastal freight is incidental as to the journey that we're underway with. And that's not because that's what it says in the act. That's really what we do. We're not a coastal operator. If it helps our customers, and they need a hand- Mm... like us being the only carrier that goes into Bluff, we do help customers on that as part of the leg, but it's not something we actively market or something we actively sell.

So I wouldn't be sitting here today saying to you that fundamentally changing the act is going to make a major difference in the way that we serve this market. I think there are certain carriers where it makes a lot of sense, and how those nodes connect, and for certain customers, it makes a lot of sense that they might have to consolidate or move ingredients from one part of the country to another part of the country for manufacturing.

And the efficiencies that would be driven by that would make a lot of sense for them. Using the same container, unpack a coastal box, clean it out, and pack it with exports makes a lot of sense in that regard for sure. Yeah. So going back to the issue of vessels getting back on time, what can be done to improve that?

And related to that, you basically said that there's a lack of capacity in the system. One of the things that sort of come through at the moment is obviously there's no regulation at the moment about the port charges. And I have actually either spent a day with the Port of Auckland the other day, which was great. But basically, they said that the limiting of the port charge effectively is the equivalent cost of the land transport to the next possible port that somebody might- Correct. Yes... might use.

If there were to be some form of Commerce Commission oversight, transparency, et cetera, involved there, you would, by the sounds of things being say, that there would need to be some factoring in of you actually need some surplus capacity. You can't take it right down to the wire because that's going to cause some significant issues.

Yeah. I would- And that capacity would then have to be paid for in that system. Yeah. I would think so. I think if you look at it in terms of the natural cargo capture for ports, right? Napier's a great example. So a large percentage, 70-plus percent of their cargo is within 20 kilometers of the port.

Whereas centre port is not the case. They have to pull cargo from all over the country. So if you have a one-size-fits-all model, you'd handicap one and benefit the other with that system being the case, right? And so the comment around it only costs as much as what-- Or we can only increase the rates as much as what it costs to get to the next port is essentially that sort of metric that's there, right?

So yes, I think if you can manage that, and I'll make no bones about it, the significant cost increases that we've seen is a contributing factor towards the challenges that we see in New Zealand today. I did some really brief numbers before I came in. If you look at the CPI increase from 2015 to today, it's around about 36% compound interest over that period of time, the increase.

And we're sitting above 50% in terms of actual cost increase in port handling itself. So port handling charges up over 50%? Yes. Yeah. So, and that's just what's been advertised out to the market using publicly available data, right? Yeah. And so you add to that then the challenges that we have around the coast with those contingencies that I spoke about and a significant increase in cost in able to, being able to, if you do a change of rotation, we're talking hundreds of thousands of dollars in terms of the amount of fuel

that we're using. If we do an omission, we have to pay for storage of those containers in the port because it's not the customer's fault that we had to omit. It's our decision that we made. Might be weather, might be whatever might be the case, but we can't go to a shipper and say to them, "We decided to omit the port. You need to pay them for the privilege of holding your cargo for a week's delay." Right? So all those costs all add up, and then you add a significant cost to serve on top of that sort of base cost.

It becomes a very difficult market to serve. So bearing in mind that if you create more capacity, and bearing in mind the comment you've already made about the efficiency of the ports handling having overall declined, are you better off or is the system, because, I mean, your charges get imposed on the cargo owners, ultimately anyway.

Would the cargo owners be better off if you actually have that extra capacity, which will cost something, than they would be at the moment with delays, out of window, potentially having to bypass ports occasionally because you can't get a window and so on? Bless you. I would say so, especially in the long run. So short term, there'd probably be a cost impact that came with that.

But if you look at that 30-year horizon that we spoke about, the challenge that we have today is it's a today problem. I mean, we can't bring a new service into Tauranga today because they don't have the space on the berth to be able to put a new service on. So that limits our ability, and that's for all carriers, right? It limits our ability to give options to shippers.

If the government's serious about the export growth that's expected, yes, definitely, it's a must. Yeah. Okay. I think I'm going to carry on as well while the other-- You know, because nobody else has got questions at the moment. I think you've kind of intimated you are committed to New Zealand long term. Yep, cool. Right.

The choice of ports served, that is a decision you make on the basis of what the customers, the cargo owners- Exactly... have decided. Okay, that's fine. Just the issue of balancing container traffic, movement of containers. Mm-hmm. Can you just give us a bit of your insight into that? Because from what we understand is, well, reefers, in particular, tend to be out- Yes... go out full. There's not a lot of demand for them coming back full. But also the movement of containers around the system. Obviously, a lot of empties turn up various

different places, and then they've got to-- They occupy space on boards, in ships- Mm-hmm... on railway wagons, et cetera, being moved around the country. Have we got that optimally ar-- What does it look like if we got that optimally arranged? Again, talking for my own business, I would say no, in terms of it being optimal. New Zealand, if you look at it purely on an import-export basis using the figs stats looks relatively well-balanced, in terms of volumes. It ebbs and flows.

Imports are a little bit down because the economy hasn't recovered as well as expected. That will grow. Exports are doing really well, so it's slightly imbalanced now, but total number- Number of containers... number of containers- Yep... roughly there or thereabouts. It's when you drop down into the equipment size types that it gets really interesting. So the imports are really predominantly 40-foot high cube imports.
